frameworks.name: Grand Slam vs Home Run Offer Trade-Off
frameworks.definition: A grand slam offer (turnkey all-in-one) closes at near-100% but limits volume; a home run offer (core product only) closes at ~75% but frees capacity and multiplies addressable deal flow.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argued that a real estate advisor with a 95% close rate is almost certainly under-pricing: close rates that high signal that the offer is so compelling relative to price that the seller is leaving substantial margin on the table, and the correct response is to raise prices substantially rather than add more services.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B high-ticket service sale
close rate at or above 90-95%
claims.mechanism: A near-100% close rate reveals that perceived value far exceeds stated price; the gap is captured by the buyer rather than the seller, so raising price transfers that surplus back to the seller without materially reducing volume.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contended that when a single acquisition channel (in this case CPA and tax-advisor referral partners) produces 60-70% of a business's revenue, the correct scaling move is to multiply the number of partners in that channel rather than diversifying into a parallel channel such as direct-to-consumer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: one channel already produces majority of revenue
channel is under-saturated (e.g., only 3-4 active partners out of a reachable pool of 40-400)
claims.mechanism: A channel producing dominant revenue shares with very few partners implies high partner-level value and untapped supply; adding partners within the proven channel compounds an already-validated model rather than betting on an unproven one.

numbers.axis: share of revenue from primary channel

bounded_by: Does not apply when the primary channel is saturated or its partners cannot be replicated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi estimated that each CPA firm sending real estate clients to Peter's business was worth roughly $500,000 to $750,000 per year in commissions, which justifies aggressive investment (time, events, speaking fees) in acquiring more CPA partners rather than building direct-to-consumer lead flow.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: real estate advisory targeting tax-motivated buyers
commission rate approximately 2.5-3%
CPA referral relationship

numbers.axis: annual commission value per CPA partner firm

bounded_by: Estimate specific to a real estate advisory at ~$55M annual deal volume and 2.5-3% commission structure

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argued that an operator who wants to exit a service line they dislike (here: Airbnb property management) should seek a partner to whom they can hand 100% operational control in exchange for a minority revenue share, provided the operator retains zero operational responsibility; accepting a meaningful revenue share while still taking client-facing accountability calls is economically irrational.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: operator has a service line they want to exit
a capable operator exists who can take full control
the partnership can be structured so the original operator has zero day-to-day obligation
claims.mechanism: Compensation for work requires effort; if all client calls still flow to the original operator because of relationship dependency, the revenue share is not passive income and the business is still founder-bottlenecked.
bounded_by: Breaks down when the client relationship is entirely tied to the original operator and cannot be transferred

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserted that in Peter's real estate advisory business, the Airbnb setup and management service is gravy rather than the core purchase driver, because the fundamental client motivation is tax reduction (cost avoidance on $1-2M annual tax liability); management ease is a convenience, not the reason they buy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: buyer is a high-income earner with $1M+ annual tax liability
real estate purchase is motivated by depreciation / tax offset rules
bounded_by: May not hold for real estate buyers motivated by investment yield rather than tax treatment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argued that dropping the turnkey management component and offering only a qualified-property-plus-referral model would convert at approximately 75% (a home run offer) rather than 95% (a grand slam offer), but by freeing the founder's time to 10x the CPA partner count, total business output would grow 8x or more.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: core value proposition (tax-motivated real estate) remains intact
founder uses recaptured time to expand CPA partner relationships
founder has sales skill sufficient to close without the turnkey bundled offer
claims.mechanism: Removing a bundled service that does not drive the core purchase decision costs roughly 25% of close rate but liberates the founder from ops-heavy management work; that time redirected to partner acquisition multiplies lead volume far beyond what the close-rate loss costs.

numbers.axis: expected business output relative to current baseline

anchors.value: ~75% close rate, 10x partner count, 8x revenue output

bounded_by: Assumes founder can sell properties to tax-motivated buyers without the management wrapper
Assumes the close-rate drop is approximately 25 percentage points, not larger

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observed that Peter's real estate business grew from roughly $10-12M to $24M to $36M to $55M annual deal volume before Airbnb management was added, indicating that the bundled management service was not the cause of prior growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: real estate advisory specializing in tax-motivated buyers
growth occurred before November of the prior year when management was added

numbers.axis: annual deal volume in Peter's real estate advisory over time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argued that when a referral partner concentration risk exists (3-4 partners providing 60-70% of revenue), the strategically correct response is to scale the number of partner relationships rather than diversify channel type, because concentration risk is solved by depth-of-channel redundancy, not channel switching.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: referral channel is proven and economics are strong
the existing channel is a type that can scale (e.g., CPA referral network rather than a single individual's endorsement)
claims.mechanism: Concentration risk in a proven channel is a partner-count problem, not a channel-type problem; switching to an unproven direct channel introduces execution risk while abandoning the validated model.

numbers.axis: number of active CPA referral partners

bounded_by: Does not apply when the referral channel itself has systemic limits (e.g., regulatory prohibition on referral fees)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contended that expectation-setting before a sale removes the management quality risk for a real estate advisor: if the client clearly understands that property management is a third-party referral rather than a guaranteed service, a management failure does not damage the advisor's core relationship or repeat-transaction pipeline.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: real estate advisory where management is a referral, not an internal service
client motivation is tax outcome (depreciation), not management convenience
claims.mechanism: Clients blame advisors for failures they were not warned about; explicit pre-sale disclosure that management is third-party transfers the psychological accountability to the client's own vetting of the manager, protecting the advisor's relationship capital.
bounded_by: Breaks down if the client's primary purchase driver is management quality rather than tax treatment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advised that a business with very high seasonal concentration (approximately 65-70% of annual revenue in Q4 for a tax-motivated real estate advisory) has a structural opportunity to smooth and grow revenue by asking what additional business is possible in the other three quarters with the same sales infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business driven by year-end tax deadlines (Q4 concentration)
sales infrastructure is already built and partially idle in Q1-Q3

numbers.axis: share of annual revenue by quarter (Peter's real estate advisory)

bounded_by: Does not apply when the seasonal concentration is driven by a regulatory deadline that cannot be changed

examples.text: Peter (a MoreMozi attendee) ran a real estate lead-generation agency for six months without changing his revenue, at which point Alex Hormozi told him to stop, get good at real estate itself, and return later. Peter spent four years selling real estate, closed roughly $125M in deals, and built a business on pace for $55M in annual volume by specializing in tax-motivated acquisitions for high-income earners using depreciation strategies. This trajectory was cited by Hormozi as evidence that domain mastery in a niche (rather than lead-gen arbitrage) is the durable path for someone whose skills fit the domain.

Peter's Airbnb management business had grown to 60 live properties when the property manager quit and handed him 20 properties with no notice. Peter brought in a client who did Airbnb arbitrage and structured a deal giving that client two-thirds of management revenue, retaining one-third. The resulting ~$100K annual income for Peter required constant operational involvement and crowded out two additional real estate sales. Hormozi used this to illustrate that a service line that distracts from the core and yields low income-per-hour should be exited or fully handed off rather than partially managed.

Peter tried introducing management partners by name to clients (e.g., 'here's my partner Ken') but clients consistently asked whether the management was under the same roof as Peter's advisory. Clients only felt comfortable with a unified brand. Hormozi acknowledged the challenge but argued it was an expectation-setting problem solvable at the front of the sales conversation rather than evidence that the management must be kept in-house.

practices.text: If a referral-partner channel is producing the majority of revenue from a small number of partners, redirect growth efforts toward finding more partners in that same channel (e.g., from 4 CPAs to 40 CPAs) before building any new channel.
When a service line distracts from the core business, test dropping it entirely and observing whether core sales hold before building infrastructure to maintain it.

When offering referral introductions instead of in-house services, frame the core value proposition (e.g., tax savings, guaranteed below-market acquisition) explicitly in the pitch so that management quality is clearly positioned as an ancillary variable rather than a promise.
